passages.text: Figure 2 : MoE pretraining at the same token budget. Two-block Monarch–Muon reaches the reported final validation loss of dense AdamW with fewer active and total parameters. Holding the Monarch factorization fixed isolates the effect of the optimizer. We compare AdamW and Muon with two and four blocks, using the same token budget and training schedule within each architecture. Dense AdamW, dense Muon, and GaLore provide reference losses for the dense quality model. The MoE comparison retains the same routing architecture and changes only the selected projections and their optimizer. Monarch–Muon achieves lower final validation loss than Monarch–AdamW in all four structured comparisons (Table 1 ). The two-block MoE reaches the reported loss of dense AdamW with 15% fewer active parameters and 25.4% fewer total parameters (767M versus 1.029B). Figure 2 places this endpoint in the training trajectory. Thus, matrix-aware updates remain useful when the optimizer acts on structured factors rather than dense weights. Increasing the block count further reduces storage, with a higher final loss under both optimizers. Dense Muon gives the lowest loss in each architecture, defining the quality reference for this representation tradeoff. The learned spectra provide a complementary view of the optimizer effect. At the same block count, Monarch–Muon retains a heavier singular-value tail than Monarch–AdamW in the gate and up projections (Figure 3 ). Similar patterns appear in additional layers and components (Appendix B ). Thus, the change in update geometry reaches the represented matrices, even though orthogonalization is local to their factors.

Figure 3 : Learned gate and up projections in layer 0 of the dense quality model. At the same block count, Muon retains larger singular values in the tail than AdamW. Additional layers and components are in Appendix B .

Structure reduces more than the optimizer state: it also compresses the trainable weights and gradients. For Muon, the smaller blocks additionally reduce the cost of orthogonalization. Section 3.2 derives the distinct scaling laws: square-factor storage decreases as 2 / m 2/m of the dense matrix, while Newton–Schulz arithmetic decreases as 2 / m 2 2/m^{2} , where m m is the block count. We test how these savings translate to allocated memory and wall time across five dense reference sizes, using four-block Monarch models and a common microbatch of four. Table 2 includes both optimizer and full-step measurements. Timings for projection-based methods exclude their periodic projection refreshes. The benefit grows with width because cheaper orthogonalization is increasingly accompanied by cheaper forward and backward passes. At 6.89B, Monarch–Muon reduces the full-step time by 45% and peak memory by 23% relative to dense Muon. Its optimizer step is 4.2 × 4.2\times faster and its state occupies 54% less memory. Figure 1 shows that both the model computations and the optimizer contribute to the full-step reduction. At this scale, Monarch–Muon also has the shortest full step and lowest peak memory among the measured state-efficient methods, even though their optimizer steps alone are cheaper. Compressing the representation therefore changes costs that optimizer-state compression leaves dense.

The smallest model marks the hardware crossover: its reduced optimizer cost does not offset the overhead of executing small factor multiplications, and peak memory is slightly higher than for dense Muon. From the 834M reference onward, Monarch–Muon improves both full-step time and peak memory relative to dense Muon. passages.text: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming k k -PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. Together, these contributions allow Ori to further push the performance and efficiency frontiers of gradient-projecting optimizers, narrowing the gap to full-rank training for LLMs. Code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Ori-Submission-2132 . 2 2 footnotetext: Purdue Institute for Cancer Research, Purdue University. 3 3 footnotetext: Department of Comparative Pathobiology, Purdue University.

We evaluate Ori’s pre-training performance against the baselines on the C4 dataset [ 26 ] using LLaMA-architecture models of four sizes (60M, 130M, 350M, and 1B), following similar experimental settings as prior work [ 14 , 39 ] . Departing from prior work that often tests a single rank, we systematically evaluate all low-rank methods across three distinct ranks for each model (e.g., r ∈ { 512,128 , 32 } r\in\{512,128,32\} for the 1B model), enabling a rigorous assessment of optimizer performance under varying degrees of memory constraints. To ensure a fair comparison, model hyperparameters were held constant for each model size, while each optimizer’s learning rate was tuned from { 0.01 , 0.005 , 0.001 , 0.0005 , 0.0001 } \{0.01,0.005,0.001,0.0005,0.0001\} . We report validation perplexity after a fixed token budget, with full details provided in Appendix E .

As shown in Table 1 , Ori’s performance is consistently strong, particularly in memory-constrained scenarios. At higher, less restrictive ranks (e.g., r = 128 r=128 for the 60M model, r = 256 r=256 for the 130M model), Ori performs on par with GaLore, establishing it as a highly competitive method in common low-rank settings. However, Ori’s distinct advantage emerges when the rank r r is severely constrained, where it demonstrates the most robust performance as its accuracy degrades the least under memory pressure. This trend, where the cost of a stale subspace projection becomes most apparent, is consistent across all model scales. For instance, when training the 130M model at an aggressively low rank of just 16, Ori achieves a validation perplexity of 43.61, substantially outperforming GaLore (60.29) and OSD (54.05). This result empirically validates our central hypothesis: actively tracking the gradient subspace drift is most critical when the optimizer has the fewest dimensions to work with. By excelling in these challenging low-rank regimes, Ori consistently narrows the performance gap to full-rank Adam, pushing the performance boundaries of memory-efficient optimization.

While the weight-subspace method ReLoRA is faster at lower ranks due to its different update mechanism, its worse model performance (see Table 1 ) highlights a clear trade-off. In contrast, Ori achieves superior model performance without compromising on speed, making it a more effective and efficient choice overall. The lightweight nature of the Oja++ update allows Ori to be both more accurate and faster than its direct competitors, making it a better choice for efficient training.

passages.text: Setup. We train the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models on 2 2 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, the 350 350 M model on 4 4 NVIDIA H20 GPUs, and the 1.3 1.3 B model on 8 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. The corresponding per-device batch sizes are 256 256 , 256 256 , 160 160 , and 160 160 , yielding global batch sizes of 512 512 , 512 512 , 640 640 , and 1280 1280 , respectively. The sequence length is 512 512 for the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models and 1024 1024 for the 350 350 M and 1.3 1.3 B models. For each model, the number of training steps approximately follows the Chinchilla scaling law ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . For example, the 1.3 1.3 B model is trained for 20480 20480 steps, which corresponds to 20480 × 1024 × 1280 ≈ 26.84 20480\times 1024\times 1280\approx 26.84 billion training tokens, or approximately 20.6 20.6 tokens per parameter. We compare our multi-stage PMRC with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , the AdamW-based GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , GoLore ( He et al., 2025 ) and Fira ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , and the Muon-based GUM ( Pan et al., 2025a ) . For projection-based methods, we set the projection rank to r = 256 r=256 and the refresh interval to 100 100 . Since GUM randomly selects a subset of layers for full-rank updates, its memory cost depends on the number of full-rank layers s s . For a fair comparison, we choose s s according to the memory budget of PMRC, setting s = 6 s=6 and r = 128 r=128 for the 60 60 M, 150 150 M, and 350 350 M models, and s = 4 s=4 and r = 128 r=128 for the 1.3 1.3 B model. The peak allocated memory for the 1.3 1.3 B model is reported in Table 6 . The detailed setup, parameter settings and additional pretraining results are deferred to Appendix E.2.2 .

Results. Table 1 presents a comparison of the training and validation losses achieved by PMRC with those achieved by AdamW, Muon, GaLore, GoLore, Fira and GUM. As evidenced by the reported results, PMRC consistently achieves the lowest training and validation losses among memory-efficient methods. The improvement supports the effectiveness of residual correction in practical LLM pretraining. PMRC also requires less optimizer-state memory than AdamW while achieving lower losses at every scale. We further evaluate the pretrained models on seven downstream benchmarks, with complete results reported in Appendix E.2.2 , where PMRC achieves the highest average accuracy among memory-efficient methods.

In this section, we provide the omitted details of the LLM supervised finetuning (SFT) experiments. For the instruction-following task, we train on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU and adopt a device micro-batch size of 16 16 with 8 8 gradient accumulation steps for Muon, GaLore, GoLore, GUM, and PMRC, and a device micro-batch size of 8 8 with 16 16 gradient accumulation steps for AdamW, so that the global batch size is 128 128 in both cases. For the mathematical reasoning task, we train on 4 4 NVIDIA H20 GPUs and adopt a device micro-batch size of 4 4 with 8 8 gradient accumulation steps for the same methods and a device micro-batch size of 2 2 with 16 16 gradient accumulation steps for AdamW, so that the global batch size is again 128 128 . For AdamW-based methods, we use the standard coefficients β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 and β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 . For Muon-based methods, the momentum coefficient is set to 1 − β = 0.95 1-\beta=0.95 with Nesterov momentum enabled. The matrix sign is approximated using 5 5 Newton–Schulz iterations, while one-dimensional parameters and embedding layers are optimized with AdamW.

Hyperparameter Tuning. For each model and optimization method we select the learning rate by a grid search over { 1 × 10 − 5 , 2 × 10 − 5 , 4 × 10 − 5 , 8 × 10 − 5 } \{1\times 10^{-5},2\times 10^{-5},4\times 10^{-5},8\times 10^{-5}\} for the instruction-following task and { 8 × 10 − 6 , 1 × 10 − 5 , 3 × 10 − 5 , 5 × 10 − 5 , 7 × 10 − 5 } \{8\times 10^{-6},1\times 10^{-5},3\times 10^{-5},5\times 10^{-5},7\times 10^{-5}\} for the mathematical-reasoning task. PMRC uses a residual cap at a ratio of 4 4 and we grid search γ ∈ { 2000 , 4000 , 8000 , 16000 } \gamma\in\{2000,4000,8000,16000\} . We select the parameters that achieve the highest accuracy on benchmarks. Additional results. We present the prompt-level and instruction-level strict accuracy on the IFEval benchmark in Table 9 . For completeness, we include the results of GUM with rank r = 256 r=256 , in addition to the memory-matched setting with r = 128 r=128 used in the main experiments. PMRC outperforms GUM at both ranks on all three models in both metrics. We also report the peak allocated GPU memory of all methods in Table 10 , measured on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU with torch.compile disabled. PMRC requires the lowest peak memory across all models. Table 10: Peak allocated GPU memory (GiB) during full-parameter SFT. We use a micro-batch size of 16 16 with 8 8 gradient accumulation steps for IFEval and a micro-batch size of 4 4 with 32 32 gradient accumulation steps for GSM8K. All memory measurements are performed on a single H20 GPU.

For all ablations, we pretrain LLaMA-150M on the C4 dataset for 9900 9900 steps with a sequence length of 512 512 and a global batch size of 512 512 . We refresh the projection basis every 100 100 steps and, unless otherwise stated, set the residual cap to ρ = 4 \rho=4 . Effect of the subspace rank. We vary the projection rank over r ∈ { 64,128,256,512 } r\in\{64,128,256,512\} with the residual weight fixed at γ = 8192 \gamma=8192 and all other settings unchanged. Increasing r r expands the subspace in which momentum is maintained and the matrix-sign transformation is applied. As shown in Figure 3 , a larger rank reduces the validation loss, but also increases the memory required to store the projection basis and the projected momentum. For a parameter matrix of size m × n m\times n , this memory cost scales as O ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ r ) O((m+n)r) . These results illustrate the trade-off between validation performance and optimizer-state memory when choosing the subspace rank. Effect of the residual weight. We fix the rank at r = 256 r=256 and vary the residual weight over γ ∈ { 0 , 1024 , 2048 , 4096 , 8192 } \gamma\in\{0,1024,2048,4096,8192\} with all other settings unchanged. Since the residual cap remains active, γ \gamma serves as an upper bound on the effective weight applied to each parameter matrix rather than its exact value. As shown in Figure 4 , the validation loss decreases monotonically as γ \gamma increases over the tested range, with diminishing improvements at larger values. In particular, γ = 0 \gamma=0 removes the residual correction and yields the highest validation loss. We investigate this performance gap through a tangent-space lens: factorized updates are confined to the tangent space of the current low-rank factors, leaving gradient components outside this space unexploited. An analysis of ten representative LoRA variants reveals that these residual components account for most of the gradient energy and exhibit strong spectral concentration. Motivated by this finding, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch and a dynamic branch to capture the principal residual gradient directions. We show that these directions define the optimal update of a local quadratic model under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints. Matrix-free randomized SVD recovers them without materializing the residual gradient, while controlled write-back preserves accumulated updates and stabilizes training within the allocated rank. DT-LoRA adds no trainable parameters or inference cost over LoRA. Experiments across computer vision and natural language processing tasks demonstrate consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants. Moreover, despite being a general-purpose adaptation method, DT-LoRA outperforms task-specific approaches to open-vocabulary domain generalization for semantic segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art results. Code is available at https://github.com/Snipine/DT-LoRA .

Large-scale pre-trained models serve as general-purpose foundations for a wide range of vision and language tasks. However, as model sizes increase, full fine-tuning becomes prohibitively expensive, requiring all model parameters to be updated and a separate set of weights to be stored for each downstream task. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) reduces this cost by freezing the pre-trained weights and optimizing only a small set of parameters [ 11 , 17 , 14 ] . Among PEFT methods, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [ 12 ] has been widely adopted for its low-rank parameterization of weight updates, which can be merged into the pre-trained weights without additional inference overhead. Nevertheless, LoRA often falls short of full fine-tuning. Prior work narrows this gap by modifying the update structure (DoRA [ 25 ] ), improving subspace initialization (PiSSA [ 26 ] , LoRA-GA [ 35 ] ), or correcting the factor gradients and optimizer states to better approximate full fine-tuning updates (LoRA-Pro [ 36 ] , AltLoRA [ 41 ] , LoFT [ 31 ] ). However, a fundamental local constraint remains: under factor perturbations δ ​ A \delta A and δ ​ B \delta B , the first-order weight update lies entirely in the tangent space defined by the current factors. The dense gradient component orthogonal to this space therefore cannot be captured by any first-order update, regardless of how the factor gradients are corrected at the current step.

To address this challenge, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch that accumulates task-specific directions as in standard LoRA and a dynamic branch that periodically absorbs principal residual directions outside the current tangent space. We prove that, under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints, the optimal update for a local quadratic model is given by the truncated SVD of the tangent-space residual gradient. Crucially, this residual inherits a factored structure from backpropagation, enabling its products with narrow matrices to be computed directly from cached input activations and output gradients. This structure allows us to construct matrix-free operators for Matrix-Free Randomized SVD, which extracts the principal residual directions via randomized SVD [ 7 ] without explicitly forming the residual gradient. To incorporate these directions while maintaining training stability, we introduce Controlled Write-back mechanism, which merges them with the current dynamic branch update, compresses the result back to the original rank, and bounds the relative change at each refresh. After training, both branches are merged into the pre-trained weights, yielding the same inference cost as standard LoRA.

We evaluate DT-LoRA across diverse vision and language tasks: the 19 image classification tasks in VTAB-1K; object detection and instance segmentation on MS COCO; open-vocabulary domain generalization for semantic segmentation (OVDG-SS) in both real-to-real and synthetic-to-real settings; eight commonsense reasoning tasks using LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA3-8B; and GLUE using DeBERTaV3-base. Under matched trainable parameter budgets, DT-LoRA consistently outperforms LoRA and its variants. On MS COCO, DT-LoRA at r = 16 r=16 achieves an average score of 46.6, exceeding LoRA at the same rank by 8.2 points and outperforming LieRA [ 29 ] , which uses twice as many trainable parameters. On OVDG-SS, DT-LoRA establishes new state-of-the-art results, surpassing the task-specific S 2 -Corr [ 46 ] despite being a general-purpose fine-tuning method. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify a geometric limitation of factorized LoRA: substantial gradient energy lies outside the current tangent space. Across ten representative LoRA variants, we show that this tangent-space residual exhibits strong spectral concentration, and establish that its truncated SVD yields the optimal update under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints for a local quadratic model. • We propose DT-LoRA, which partitions a fixed rank budget into Stable and Dynamic branches to incorporate principal residual directions. Matrix-Free Randomized SVD extracts these directions without materializing the residual gradient, while Controlled Write-back integrates them with accumulated updates and bounds the change at each refresh, enabling dynamic tangent-space adaptation without additional trainable parameters or inference overhead.

• We demonstrate the effectiveness of DT-LoRA across diverse vision and language tasks, with consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants under matched trainable parameter budgets. On OVDG-SS, DT-LoRA outperforms task-specific methods and establishes new state-of-the-art results.

On GLUE ( Tab. 6 ), DT-LoRA achieves the highest average score of 88.7, outperforming LoRA under the same parameter budget by 1.1 points and AdaLoRA, which uses more trainable parameters, by 0.6 points. It also surpasses full fine-tuning (88.3) while training less than 1% of the model parameters. The largest improvement over LoRA is observed on QQP, with a gain of 3.6 points.

passages.text: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present Idea2Prior, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

The central design separates inexpensive assessment of a broad candidate pool from a bounded examination of document evidence. After abstract assessment and citation expansion, an Expert model jointly considers up to 60 candidates. Five papers are selected for PDF acquisition; unavailable PDFs are not replaced by additional papers in retrieval-only mode. Complete available abstracts remain in the Expert input, along with evidence availability and up to six locally selected PDF passages per acquired paper. A missing PDF does not make a paper irrelevant and does not prevent it from ranking first. The optional full-report mode retains downstream synthesis for users who need a written literature analysis. The revised evaluation covers 30 query cases: ten from each of three prompt tiers, with shared targets across tiers. The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research. The ChatGPT total includes one convention-based credit, disclosed in Section 5.1 . Idea2Prior leads both baselines by 20 percentage points on EASY and MEDIUM, but trails ChatGPT by 10 points on HARD. Mean selected-run latency is 8.89 minutes, and a separately reported nine-query cost sample averages $0.0945. Thus the present evidence shows a recovery advantage in two tiers and a low observed API cost, with longer latency than the supplied browser averages. Our contributions are: 1. An auditable retrieval-and-ranking workflow with identity-aware candidate records, semantic citation filtering, and a joint Top 5 decision over a bounded shortlist.

The released benchmark contains 30 queries in each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD. According to the dataset construction record, GPT-6 Astra in ChatGPT was used to extract and generate the shared literature-search prompts. EASY supplies more identifying detail, MEDIUM removes some detail, and HARD uses shorter, less specific descriptions. These are intended difficulty levels rather than independently calibrated labels. The tiers are not independent paper pools; in particular, MEDIUM and HARD share targets with different wording. The present comparison uses the first ten IDs of each tier: EASY N001–N010, MEDIUM C001–C010, and HARD C001–C010. Each system receives the same filled item prompt: a paper-finding instruction, the 2015–2025 publication/verified-version constraint, up-to-five distinct works with exact bibliographic fields and a short match explanation, identity verification and deduplication requirements, and the idea text. The designated target is not supplied to retrieval. Original prompts and outputs are preserved; Appendix A gives the exact shared wrappers and a three-tier example. These are retrieval prompts, distinct from the internal scoring prompts. ChatGPT and Gemini were tested through their October 2026 web Deep Research interfaces; backend model/build identifiers and subscription tiers were not recorded. Idea2Prior used its API pipeline. Preserved Expert outputs identify the configured alias openai/gemini-3.8-flash ; a compatibility-protocol alias does not independently verify the upstream served model. The released native-Gemini preset is not a newly benchmarked replacement for those historical runs.

Results use final selected runs, including authorized replacements of operationally failed attempts. They therefore measure selected-result recovery, not first-attempt reliability. EASY initially produced five target hits over ten planned queries before recovery; the final selection produced nine. We retain the historical ChatGPT EASY convention of 7/10: six observed hits plus one convention-based counted hit. No returned paper or intersection is fabricated for that credit. Counting only observed hits would make ChatGPT EASY 6/10 and aggregate recovery 12/30; our primary table preserves the earlier agreed convention explicitly. passages.text: Setup. We train the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models on 2 2 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, the 350 350 M model on 4 4 NVIDIA H20 GPUs, and the 1.3 1.3 B model on 8 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. The corresponding per-device batch sizes are 256 256 , 256 256 , 160 160 , and 160 160 , yielding global batch sizes of 512 512 , 512 512 , 640 640 , and 1280 1280 , respectively. The sequence length is 512 512 for the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models and 1024 1024 for the 350 350 M and 1.3 1.3 B models. For each model, the number of training steps approximately follows the Chinchilla scaling law ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . For example, the 1.3 1.3 B model is trained for 20480 20480 steps, which corresponds to 20480 × 1024 × 1280 ≈ 26.84 20480\times 1024\times 1280\approx 26.84 billion training tokens, or approximately 20.6 20.6 tokens per parameter. We compare our multi-stage PMRC with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , the AdamW-based GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , GoLore ( He et al., 2025 ) and Fira ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , and the Muon-based GUM ( Pan et al., 2025a ) . For projection-based methods, we set the projection rank to r = 256 r=256 and the refresh interval to 100 100 . Since GUM randomly selects a subset of layers for full-rank updates, its memory cost depends on the number of full-rank layers s s . For a fair comparison, we choose s s according to the memory budget of PMRC, setting s = 6 s=6 and r = 128 r=128 for the 60 60 M, 150 150 M, and 350 350 M models, and s = 4 s=4 and r = 128 r=128 for the 1.3 1.3 B model. The peak allocated memory for the 1.3 1.3 B model is reported in Table 6 . The detailed setup, parameter settings and additional pretraining results are deferred to Appendix E.2.2 .

Results. Table 1 presents a comparison of the training and validation losses achieved by PMRC with those achieved by AdamW, Muon, GaLore, GoLore, Fira and GUM. As evidenced by the reported results, PMRC consistently achieves the lowest training and validation losses among memory-efficient methods. The improvement supports the effectiveness of residual correction in practical LLM pretraining. PMRC also requires less optimizer-state memory than AdamW while achieving lower losses at every scale. We further evaluate the pretrained models on seven downstream benchmarks, with complete results reported in Appendix E.2.2 , where PMRC achieves the highest average accuracy among memory-efficient methods.

Setup. We train the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models on 2 2 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, the 350 350 M model on 4 4 NVIDIA H20 GPUs, and the 1.3 1.3 B model on 8 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. The corresponding per-device batch sizes are 256 256 , 256 256 , 160 160 , and 160 160 , yielding global batch sizes of 512 512 , 512 512 , 640 640 , and 1280 1280 , respectively. The sequence length is 512 512 for the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models and 1024 1024 for the 350 350 M and 1.3 1.3 B models. For each model, the number of training steps approximately follows the Chinchilla scaling law ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . For example, the 1.3 1.3 B model is trained for 20480 20480 steps, which corresponds to 20480 × 1024 × 1280 ≈ 26.84 20480\times 1024\times 1280\approx 26.84 billion training tokens, or approximately 20.6 20.6 tokens per parameter. We compare our multi-stage PMRC with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , the AdamW-based GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , GoLore ( He et al., 2025 ) and Fira ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , and the Muon-based GUM ( Pan et al., 2025a ) . For projection-based methods, we set the projection rank to r = 256 r=256 and the refresh interval to 100 100 . Since GUM randomly selects a subset of layers for full-rank updates, its memory cost depends on the number of full-rank layers s s . For a fair comparison, we choose s s according to the memory budget of PMRC, setting s = 6 s=6 and r = 128 r=128 for the 60 60 M, 150 150 M, and 350 350 M models, and s = 4 s=4 and r = 128 r=128 for the 1.3 1.3 B model. The peak allocated memory for the 1.3 1.3 B model is reported in Table 6 . The detailed setup, parameter settings and additional pretraining results are deferred to Appendix E.2.2 .

Results. Table 1 presents a comparison of the training and validation losses achieved by PMRC with those achieved by AdamW, Muon, GaLore, GoLore, Fira and GUM. As evidenced by the reported results, PMRC consistently achieves the lowest training and validation losses among memory-efficient methods. The improvement supports the effectiveness of residual correction in practical LLM pretraining. PMRC also requires less optimizer-state memory than AdamW while achieving lower losses at every scale. We further evaluate the pretrained models on seven downstream benchmarks, with complete results reported in Appendix E.2.2 , where PMRC achieves the highest average accuracy among memory-efficient methods.

Following the standard practical implementation of Muon, we retain the shape-dependent learning-rate scaling factor 0.2 ​ max ⁡ { m , n } 0.2\sqrt{\max\{m,n\}} and weight decay with coefficient λ \lambda . These two components are inherited from Liu et al. (2025) . We set ρ = 4 \rho=4 and ϵ = 10 − 30 \epsilon=10^{-30} in our experiments. Second, periodic SVD computations in GaLore introduce time overhead when the projection basis is refreshed, particularly for high-dimensional matrices. To improve computational efficiency, we replace the exact SVD with a warm-started subspace approximation adapted from ARO ( Gong et al., 2026 ) . decision.reason: The seven selections cover the profile’s strongest priorities: LoRA geometry, weight-update spectra, memory-efficient LLM training, and research-digest retrieval. The main unresolved uncertainty is whether an unseen paper directly tests training for low-rank weight compressibility; the focused searches here did not surface one. Further available actions are unlikely to displace these supported choices. I resolved the reviewers’ material disagreement about BMuon using inspection: its compression target is MLP-channel pruning, not low-rank weight factorization. Narrower RLVR, continual-learning, and phone-NPU papers therefore do not take a slot.
